_At this time last year, I[wrote about a question](https://zeteo.com/p/how-to-
talk-about-politics-thanksgiving) very dear to me: how we speak to one
another, how we love one another, and thus, how we exist as political beings.
I referred to Zohran Mamdani and Donald Trump's surprisingly warm relationship
as a loose demonstration of what I was getting at. Since then, that
relationship has continued, much to Mamdani's benefit. _

_All the while, as we enter the holiday season, and approach 2028 - and many
people you know are already adopting Pundit Brain instead of just saying what
they think - my argument is, for better or for worse, relevant once again.
That's why we are resharing my piece on how to talk about politics at
Thanksgiving with people you love. I'd love to hear your response to it in the
comments below. _

* * *

Every Thanksgiving, at least in the U.S., there's routine fodder plated up as
an appetizer: 'Here's what experts say'-style articles providing tips to
script away discomfort. _Be careful whom you invite. You don 't have to argue
about everything. Agree to disagree. Leave politics off the table. Compromise.
_And so forth.

This advice is not always necessarily wrong. But the genre feels mere degrees
away from the guidance politicians get from overpaid suits-and-ties: _Sanitize
your views, preempt tough conversations, smooth over possible friction by
'meeting someone where they are'_ (which they ultimately translate to mean _'
watering yourself down'_). It's all about appearing pragmatic, respectable,
realistic.

Sometimes, it feels like we put on those ties, too. Instead of just saying
what we think, we hyper-focus on what we believe other people think. Fixating
on polls and odds and whether something helps a political party overshadows
the stakes of an issue itself.

We don't talk about displaced migrants, we talk about campaign ads. We don't
talk about poisoned lakes or dying bees, we talk about how a hypothetical
median voter feels about kids defacing a glass-protected painting in an act of
climate-inspired protest. We don't talk about 20,000 killed children in Gaza,
we talk about how discussing _this_ or _that_ does not help your cause.

Political discussions can end up being so steeped in secondhand opinion it
becomes unclear what we ourselves think. And when we behave this way, we
actually aren't fueling this "more productive" discourse we're told we create
by diluting ourselves. We're simply mimicking the same political class that's
helped make us feel so polarized, and so unproductive, in the first place.

So, my Thanksgiving plea: Just say what _you_ think! Stop behaving like unpaid
political consultants and pollsters and party cogs!

And we have an ongoing example of what this looks like in practice, at least
for elected officials: Zohran Mamdani and Donald Trump.

### **Showing How It 's Done**

Last year, Mamdani went to the Oval Office, amid earlier threats by Trump to
pull funding from New York City and to deploy troops to it. My interest in the
meeting was not in psychoanalyzing the president's[ surprising
warmth](https://zeteo.com/p/donald-trump-zohran-mamdani-white-house-
meeting?utm_medium=email) toward the New York City mayor-elect. Politics, as
Trump's shown us for a decade, is wrapped up in performance, and the
connoisseur himself is doubtful to forget that. And performance is something
all __ politicians participate in. They're modeling aesthetic and behavior as
a signal to other politicians and big media and lobbyists - and downwards, to
journalists and commentators and ultimately the rest of us.

Let's consider Mamdani's signaling. In a room crowded with more reporters than
some world-leader visits, the 34-year-old mayor-elect didn't falter. He didn't
back down on his positions. He didn't even take back calling Trump a fascist!
He was walking a tightrope, seeking to show both Trump - and importantly,
everyone else - he was there to advocate for his constituents. But that didn't
lead him to preemptively show himself as malleable, chameleonic. Heck, he
straight-up condemned Israel's genocide of Palestinians, right next to a man
complicit in it.

Mamdani earnestly appealed to Trump's _purported_ focus on common goals like
affordability and their mutual love of New York. He used that commonality as
an entry point, such that even if he hadn't connected with Trump, he at least
would've connected with those watching. He didn't sanitize Trump, or even say
Trump was actually _achieving_ his purported goals. Pragmatism didn't
necessitate losing himself. He stood by his convictions, maintaining what drew
people to him in the first place: authenticity.

### **Pull Up a Chair to the Kitchen Table**

"Authenticity" - like "affordability" and its cousin, "kitchen-table issues" -
have been haplessly tossed around consultancy offices like hacky sacks for
years, especially after Trump's defeat of Hillary Clinton in 2016. Mamdani's
campaign succeeded in making these words mean more than just prop jargon.

He does this by laying his cards out, and inviting you to join in the next
hand. _I feel this way about X.[Regardless of your views on it, I want you to
be cared for](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/Lp-PQghdNO8), I want you to
afford to live in my city. _The entry point that enables him to reach someone
who may disagree with him still nevertheless clearly reflects his morals. And
because that entry point is tied to his broader moral universe, Mamdani can
bring someone closer to him and his other convictions, without having to
apologize for them.

Virginia Woolf once wrote: "If you do not tell the truth about yourself you
cannot tell it about other people." She wrote it as a critique of the literary
"ivory tower," of those whose perspectives may be distant from those they're
writing about. That, failing to see your own complexities, positive or
negative, would distort your sense of reality and thus your perception of
others.

This applies to us - with our own background and experiences and perspective -
trying to connect and commiserate with another who carries all their own. I
can't fairly meet you where you are, without recognizing I may not know __
where you are. And I can't hope for you to _meet_ _me (_ or for us to meet
_each other_) if I mislead you on where _I_ am.

Some of our fears regarding political conversation revolve around
respectability. Well, I find it respectful to treat others as you would
yourself. If you see yourself as capable of absorbing information, analyzing
it, and responding sincerely, you ought to extend that to others. Diluting
yourself in anticipation of what you suppose is more palatable to another is
_actually_ what's disrespectful - to you and to them.

As a reporter in Washington, DC, I've witnessed how disrespectfully the media
and political apparatus view people: as static, as fixed in their views - as
data on charts that determine whether to even bother to appeal to them. That
cynical attitude trickles downward - into articles we read, talking heads we
listen to, and finally into us, especially if we put on those suits and ties
and start absorbing that attitude, too.

This attitude discourages curiosity. It disregards the reality that we shape
each other. It forecloses the possibility that we could be for each other, and
not simply in spite of each other. It's anti-political.

The word "politics" can make you tense up. But the act of politics - imagining
a vision, and trying to bring others to believe in it too - is actually quite
beautiful. But you can't do it if you view people as static, as people to
placate rather than bring closer to you.

My own worldview has shifted a bunch - shaped by the places I've lived, the
people I've met, the experiences that have challenged and clarified me.
Through all that, I've found a throughline of humility, softness, generosity.
Those attitudes have served me better than seeing the world as fixed, as
composites of polls and predicted behaviors and things that are beyond my
grasp. It's been more empowering to know that since I've changed, so can
someone else, and I can be part of that just as much as they've been for me.

Empathy, or meeting someone where they are, is not at odds with conviction.
Welcoming someone into your moral universe is much more powerful than trying
to disguise it out of anticipation that they don't deserve the dignity of your
full self.

This rubric applies to elected officials, surely. But I'm concerned more so
with the rest of us - because I think we're usually _better_ at earnest
political discourse than the political machinery that looks at us so
cynically. It seems we only get worse when we absorb their own cynical habits.

James Baldwin is attributed as saying: "If I love you, I have to make you
conscious of the things that you do not see." If you find yourself alongside
friends or family you may disagree with over the holidays, realize there may
be at least one commonality, one entry point that can bring you closer to
them: love.

[Share](https://zeteo.com/p/how-to-actually-talk-about-politics-at-
thanksgiving-2026?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

And if your love and your graciousness can help bring those around you a
little closer to the rest of your moral universe, the conversation might just
feel a bit more heartening, and a bit less dreadful.

The holiday season can hold many conflicting, potent emotions for us. The hope
is, in the mix of all that, we get at least a moment of sacred stillness, to
step back from life, look at it, and feel moved by all the love and beauty
inside it. What better time to make our world feel closer, our discourse feel
softer, than when we may feel most sentimental, reverent of the best parts of
our lives - and surrounded by some of them?
